points.name: 〜おかげで (okage de) — thanks to / owing to (positive result)
points.shortDescription: Credits a cause with a positive outcome: 'thanks to X, Y (good thing) happened'.
points.formation: Verb/い-adj (plain form) + おかげで  |  Noun + の + おかげで  |  な-adj + な + おかげで
points.explanation:
おかげで is the grammar of gratitude — 'thanks to X, a good thing happened.' 先生[せんせい]のおかげで合格[ごうかく]できました: 'Thanks to my teacher, I was able to pass' — the teacher's contribution made the good outcome possible and deserves acknowledgment. The cause can be a person, situation, or ongoing action. Its mirror image for negative results is せいで (blame) — learn them as a pair.

One delightful quirk: おかげで can be used sarcastically in spoken Japanese. 彼[かれ]のおかげで、仕事[しごと]が増[ふ]えた — said with the right tone, that means 'Thanks to him (not).' The sarcasm works precisely because おかげで is so strongly associated with genuine gratitude that inverting it lands with a wry punch. The standalone おかげさまで ('thanks to you / to everyone') is a staple of everyday polite Japanese — one of those expressions worth having ready in any conversation.
rules: Noun + の + おかげで = thanks to [noun] (positive outcome — gratitude)
Plain form + おかげで = thanks to the fact that (positive result follows)
Counterpart: せいで (because of — negative outcome, blame)
Can be used sarcastically in spoken Japanese — context and tone make it clear
Standalone: おかげで / おかげさまで = thanks to you/everyone (gratitude phrase)

points.flashcardAnswer: Credits a cause with a positive outcome: 'thanks to X, Y (good thing) happened'.

practice.prompt: What does 〜おかげで mean?
choices: because of X (negative result)
thanks to X / owing to X — attributes a POSITIVE outcome to a cause
despite X
just because X
practice.explanation: 〜おかげで = thanks to / owing to X (positive). 先生[せんせい]のおかげで合格[ごうかく]できた = thanks to my teacher, I was able to pass. The cause (teacher's help) is credited with a good outcome. Compare: せいで = negative attribution.

practice.explanation: Noun + の + おかげで: サポートの + おかげで = thanks to the support. イベントが成功[せいこう]した = the event succeeded. おかげで is used for positive outcomes; the support is credited.

points.name: 〜せいで (sei de) — because of (negative result / blame)
points.shortDescription: Attributes a negative outcome to a cause — with a tone of blame or complaint.
points.formation: Verb/い-adj (plain form) + せいで  |  Noun + の + せいで  |  な-adj + な + せいで
points.explanation:
せいで is おかげで's counterpart — it attributes a negative outcome to a cause, with a clear undertone of blame or complaint. 雨[あめ]のせいで試合[しあい]が中止[ちゅうし]になった: 'Because of the rain, the match was cancelled' — the rain is responsible, and the speaker is not pleased about it. When the cause is a person (彼[かれ]のせいで — 'because of him'), using せいで points a finger directly at them, so be aware of the social charge when using it in conversation about others.

Importantly, you can turn the blame on yourself too: 自分[じぶん]のせいで失敗[しっぱい]した ('It was my own fault I failed') — self-recrimination with せいで is completely natural.

Register note: if you want to express a negative cause without the accusatory sting — in a neutral explanation rather than a complaint — ために (because of) is the more diplomatic choice. せいで always carries the implication of 'and I'm assigning responsibility for this.'
rules: Noun + の + せいで = because of [noun] (negative result — blame directed at noun)
Plain form + せいで = because of the fact that (negative result, blame)
Implies the cause is at fault — using it about a person carries social weight
Compare: おかげで (positive result, gratitude) ↔ せいで (negative result, blame)
Neutral alternative for negative cause: ために (no blame nuance)

points.name: 〜ことから (koto kara) — from the fact that / because
points.shortDescription: Draws a conclusion, observation, or name from a fact or characteristic.
points.formation: Plain form + ことから + conclusion or explanation
points.explanation:
ことから is the grammar of reasoned inference — it draws a conclusion, observation, deduction, or even a naming from a fact or observable characteristic. 形[かたち]が富士山[ふじさん]に似[に]ていることから、この山[やま]は「ミニ富士[ふじ]」と呼[よ]ばれています: 'From the fact that its shape resembles Mt. Fuji, this mountain is called Mini Fuji' — the name is derived from the observable characteristic. 彼女[かのじょ]が落[お]ち着[つ]いていることから、すでに知[し]っていたのではないかと思[おも]いました — 'From the fact that she was so calm, I inferred she already knew' — the observation grounds the deduction.

This derivation-from-evidence flavor is what distinguishes ことから from plain から or ので, which express more direct causation. ことから specifically marks a logical step from observable characteristic to conclusion, inference, or origin. It's formal and analytical in register — most at home in explanatory writing, origin stories, historical explanations, and academic reasoning.
rules: Plain form + ことから = from the fact that / because (drawing a conclusion from a fact)
Often used to explain origins, names, customs derived from observable characteristics
More formal than から; used in explanatory, observational, academic contexts
The conclusion is typically an inference, name, or custom derived from the stated fact
Compare: ので/から = direct cause; ことから = derived conclusion from an observable characteristic

examples.japanese: 色[いろ]が白[しろ]いことから、その鳥[とり]は「白鷺[しらさぎ]」と呼[よ]ばれています。
examples.romaji: Iro ga shiroi koto kara, sono tori wa 'shirasagi' to yobarete imasu.
examples.english: From the fact that its color is white, that bird is called 'shirasagi' (great egret).

examples.japanese: 多[おお]くの文化[ぶんか]で食事[しょくじ]は共[とも]に行[おこな]うことから、料理[りょうり]は人[ひと]をつなぐものと言[い]われています。
examples.romaji: Ooku no bunka de shokuji wa tomo ni okonau koto kara, ryouri wa hito wo tsunagu mono to iwarete imasu.
examples.english: From the fact that meals are shared together in many cultures, food is said to be something that connects people.

examples.japanese: 彼女[かのじょ]が落[お]ち着[つ]いていることから、すでに知[し]っていたのではないかと思[おも]いました。
examples.romaji: Kanojo ga ochitsuite iru koto kara, sudeni shitte ita no dewa nai ka to omoimashita.
examples.english: From the fact that she was calm, I thought she might have already known.

examples.japanese: この地域[ちいき]は夏[なつ]でも涼[すず]しいことから、避暑地[ひしょち]として人気[にんき]があります。

practice.prompt: What does 〜ことから mean?
choices: because of / since (same as から)
from the fact that / based on the fact that — draws a conclusion, deduction, or observation from a fact or characteristic
just because (regret)
thanks to (positive)

practice.prompt: Which correctly says 'From the fact that the lights are on, someone must be home'?

practice.prompt: Which means 'From the fact that its leaves are yellowing, we can tell this plant is sick'?

practice.explanation: Plain form + ことから: なっている + ことから = from the fact that (leaves are yellowing). 病気[びょうき]だとわかる = can tell it's sick. ことから marks that the observation (yellowing leaves) is the basis for the deduction.

practice.prompt: Which correctly says 'Because it was discovered by a Dutch person, this route is called the Dutch Route'?

オランダ人[ひと]によって発見[はっけん]されたのに、この道[みち]はオランダ道[みち]と呼[よ]ばれている。
practice.explanation: Past form + ことから: 発見[はっけん]された + ことから = from the fact that it was discovered. オランダ道[みち]と呼[よ]ばれている = is called the Dutch Route. Naming/etymology explanation — classic ことから use.

practice.prompt: What TYPES of conclusions typically follow ことから?
choices: Only direct causes and effects — and this holds in every register, formal or casual.
Deductions, naming explanations, or observations drawn from characteristics or facts
Regrets about past actions
Hypothetical outcomes
practice.explanation: ことから is used for: (1) naming/etymology: 形[かたち]が丸[まる]いことからテニスボールと呼[よ]ぶ; (2) deductions/inferences: 証拠[しょうこ]がないことから犯人[はんにん]とは言[い]えない; (3) observations drawn from characteristics. It signals reasoned inference, not simple causation.

practice.prompt: Which correctly says 'From the fact that it has no ID, we cannot identify this person'?
choices: 身分[みぶん]証[しょう]がないことから、この人物[じんぶつ]の身元[みもと]が確認[かくにん]できない。

practice.prompt: Which means 'From the fact that it looks like a cat's paw, this confection is called Nekoashi-mochi'?

practice.explanation: Plain form + ことから: 似[に]ている + ことから = from the fact that (resembles). ネコ手[て]餅[もち]と呼[よ]ばれている = is called Nekoashi-mochi. Naming explanation — ことから signals the etymology based on visual similarity.

practice.prompt: Which correctly says 'From the fact that evidence was discovered, the investigation advanced'?
choices: 証拠[しょうこ]が発見[はっけん]されたことから、捜査[そうさ]が進展[しんてん]した。
証拠[しょうこ]が発見[はっけん]されたから、捜査[そうさ]が進展[しんてん]した。
証拠[しょうこ]が発見[はっけん]されたせいで、捜査[そうさ]が進展[しんてん]した。
証拠[しょうこ]が発見[はっけん]されたので、捜査[そうさ]が進展[しんてん]した。
practice.explanation: Past form + ことから: 発見[はっけん]された + ことから = from the fact that (evidence was found). 捜査[そうさ]が進展[しんてん]した = investigation advanced. ことから marks the discovery as the factual basis for the development.

practice.prompt: What is the DIFFERENCE between ことから and から?
choices: They are completely identical
ことから = the basis is a fact/observation; used for deductions, naming, or reasoned inference (more formal/analytical); から = simple cause ('because X, Y')
ことから is only for written Japanese
から can only be used with い-adjectives, with no exceptions in modern standard Japanese — textbooks treat this as an absolute rule.
practice.explanation: ことから is more analytical — it signals 'the following conclusion is drawn from this observable fact.' から is a simpler 'because': 疲[つか]れているから眠[ねむ]い (I'm tired so sleepy — simple cause). 疲[つか]れているようなことから、体調不良[たいちょうふりょう]かもしれない (from the apparent fatigue, may be unwell — deductive reasoning).

practice.prompt: Which correctly says 'From the fact that it grows in shade, this plant is called the Shadow Flower'?

practice.prompt: Which means 'From the fact that the door is unlocked, someone might have entered'?

practice.prompt: Which correctly says 'From the fact that this word is of foreign origin, it is written in katakana'?

practice.prompt: Which sentences shows ことから used for ETYMOLOGY/NAMING (the most classic use)?

points.name: 〜ばかりに (bakari ni) — solely because / just because (regrettable result)
points.shortDescription: Pins a bad outcome on one specific, often unfortunate, reason.
points.formation: Plain form + ばかりに + negative/unfortunate outcome
points.explanation:
ばかりに is regret bottled into grammar — it singles out one specific cause as the sole, unfortunate reason a bad outcome occurred. 'All because of / simply because / just because.' あの一言[ひとこと]を言[い]ったばかりに、関係[かんけい]が壊[こわ]れてしまった: 'All because I said that one thing, the relationship fell apart.' If only that single action hadn't happened, everything would be fine.

The nuance is sharp: ばかりに pins the entire bad outcome on this one factor — no shared responsibility, no other contributing causes. This emphasis on singular causation and the strong sense of regret (often self-recrimination) distinguishes it from せいで, which is broader in its attribution of blame.

ばかりに is literary and formal, appearing more often in writing and reflective speech than casual conversation. Think of it as the grammar of 'that one moment I wish I could take back.'
rules: Plain form + ばかりに = all because of / just because (one regrettable cause → bad result)
Main clause must be a negative or regrettable outcome
Implies the cause alone (no other factors) is responsible for the bad result
Carries a strong nuance of regret or self-blame
More literary and formal than せいで; emphasizes the singular nature of the cause

practice.explanation: Verb past + ばかりに: 言[い]った + ばかりに = all because I told (the truth). こじれてしまった = things got complicated. The irony: honesty led to complications.
